Hiding in plain sight

By: Joy Summers | Commission

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

Unique Selling Point:
Unique high ranking sources - one prepared to go on camera - with a view that challenges the prevailing narrative

Summary:
In early July, the KZN deputy police commissioner Nhlanhla Mkhwanazi shook the very foundations of the state during a press conference that looked more like a coup than a Sunday afternoon press conference. He arrived in camo gear flanked by bodyguards with semi-automatic machine guns slung across their chests.

His message to the South African public was that the criminal justice system was corrupt and something needed to be done urgently. It’s not that the public didn’t know this, but coming from a high ranking general in the SAPS it carried an enormous amount of weight. And the police are notorious for saying nothing, so this press conference was explosive. Mkhwanazi named names, showed pieces of evidence, and overnight he became the heroic whistleblower, propelled almost to mythical status for a public worn down by crime and corruption.

During the long briefing he made allegations against the police minister, municipal cops, top cops, the judiciary and a host of others. In response the President called for a commission of inquiry, put the police minister Senzo Mchunu on special leave and General Shadrack Sibiya who has been in line for the top job of the Hawks was suspended, his name tainted by the allegations. Sibiya’s legal papers challenging his suspension run to almost 2000 pages, and tell a completely different story, but he lost on urgency and will have to wait for his time at the commission to reveal his secrets- secrets which are just as eye popping as Mkhwanazi’s revelations.

Voice over One

VO 1
This is the headquarters of SAPS Crime Intelligence. The people who work here are sworn to secrecy.

Tasked with ensuring our national security, it’s where organized criminals are spied on, where intelligence is gathered and threats to the state identified.

But, in recent years, it’s become a battleground as determined officers hold the line against looters and dirty politicians.

At stake seems to be a covert budget of hundreds of millions of Rands. Officially known as the Secret Service account, it’s used to pay for informants and undercover operations.

And it’s highly vulnerable to abuse.

Mpho Kwinika
It's not accounted for. You can spend money there, you can lie! And use it for projects, and you will not know about it

In the past few weeks, sources we’ve spoken to say this secret account, is at the heart of the power struggle plaguing our criminal justice system; one now thrust into the public eye by a Provincial Police Commissioner, widely hailed as a national hero.

General Mkhwanazi
I will fight this fight until the end. Whatever the end is, we will fight.

Govan

Lets agree that it is control of the slush fund, because if you want to win the elections you have to use that money.

It’s a complex picture now being probed by the Madlanga Commission of Inquiry into an apparently compromised criminal justice system.

metadata.Summary: In early July, the KZN deputy police commissioner Nhlanhla Mkhwanazi shook the very foundations of the state during a press conference that looked more like a coup than a Sunday afternoon press conference. He arrived in camo gear flanked by bodyguards with semi-automatic machine guns slung across their chests. His message to the South African public was that the criminal justice system was corrupt and something needed to be done urgently. It’s not that the public didn’t know this, but coming from a high ranking general in the SAPS it carried an enormous amount of weight. And the police are notorious for saying nothing, so this press conference was explosive. Mkhwanazi named names, showed pieces of evidence, and overnight he became the heroic whistleblower, propelled almost to mythical status for a public worn down by crime and corruption. During the long briefing he made allegations against the police minister, municipal cops, top cops, the judiciary and a host of others. In response the President called for a commission of inquiry, put the police minister Senzo Mchunu on special leave and General Shadrack Sibiya who has been in line for the top job of the Hawks was suspended, his name tainted by the allegations. Sibiya’s legal papers challenging his suspension run to almost 2000 pages, and tell a completely different story, but he lost on urgency and will have to wait for his time at the commission to reveal his secrets- secrets which are just as eye popping as Mkhwanazi’s revelations.
